FINDINGS:
• The Vedic accent left almost no trace in NIA vowels. All 12 groups tested accent against syllable position and weight for pretonic shortening, lengthening, apocope, syncope, r̩ and vowel quality. Position or weight wins nearly everywhere. Compensatory lengthening follows the first syllable (Marathi, Bhil, Eastern, Rajasthani–Gujarati) or the modern stressed syllable (Hindi belt), never the Vedic accent. What survives is small and scattered: Hindi final -u > -ū except under the accent (áśru > ā̃sū, bāhú > bāh), oxytone -í kept through apocope in western Tharu, Pashai lengthening of the accented vowel in disyllables, and a Palula drag chain in which only accented ā becomes ō. Khowar does the opposite of Tharu, losing accented final -i/-u, so even the final-vowel effect has no single direction. A second, accent-aware score settles where the modern accent comes from: in all 32 lects whose sources mark accent, a positional rule (the old penult before apocope, the last syllable after it, or the first syllable) beats the Vedic accent carried through the chain by 0.03–0.12; the Vedic accent beats no accent by at most 0.01. See the accent grid and accent table.
  • Subgroups from shared rule-list prefixes (innovations only, rules never pooled). Each chain lists only changes away from OIA, so a retention can never group lects, and a change is one exact rule, so differently conditioned rules (s > h vs s > h / V _ V) never count as shared. Putting every chain's rules in one canonical order (most widespread first) and asking how long a prefix two lects share gives a tree whose first split separates Dardic + Romani/Domari (plain degemination, anusvāra lost) from the rest; within the rest, early MIA (Pali, Aśokan, Kharoṣṭhī) separates from a mainland defined by C + r/ḣ and stop + stop assimilation and intervocalic stop loss. The strict prefix tree is too fragile to read, and below the top levels the tree largely reproduces the agent groups, whose chains share wording as well as history. See the prefix tree.
  • Round 2 found a few new shared innovations in the vowels. Medial u > a helps all 8 core Bhil lects and hurts every other lect, a clean Bhil-core isogloss. Kati and Kamviri share two vowel shifts (ā > o in the new final syllable, a > u in monosyllables) that every other Nuristani lect rejects. Romani a > e in open first syllables (blocked before labials) unites Welsh, Balkan and Zargari against Lomavren and Domari. Odia alone nasalises V m V (kumāra > kuā̃ra).
  • One family-wide skeleton of relative chronology comes out of the data. Across all 151 chains, the order of pairs of changes was tested by moving each rule past the other. The cluster assimilations and sibilant merger come first. Intervocalic lenition follows, then degemination and compensatory lengthening, then loss of final vowels. Counting each lect's own rules, intervocalic stop loss must precede degemination in 120 lects with none against, and compensatory lengthening must precede apocope in 45 lects with 2 against. At the level of single changes (one definition shared across lects in changes.sc; nothing pooled by tag), int-stop-loss.kgcjtdy ({k g c j t d y} > ∅ / V _ V) precedes degem-plain.g (G $1 > $2) in 66 lects with none against, and the sibilant merger Sib > s precedes kṣ > kkʰ in 80 with none against.
  • Lenition before cluster reduction holds in every branch. What differs is how clusters reduce. Mainland MIA made geminates, which resisted lenition and simplified much later. Dardic, Nuristani and (partly) Romani never geminated, but their clusters still simplified only after lenition (41 lects for, 0 against, counting each lect's own rules). This is the clearest structural split between Dardic and the mainland.
  • The MIA stages separate cleanly. Pali and Aśokan reject every Prakrit lenition (adding intervocalic stop loss costs +0.058 NED). The Kharoṣṭhī texts keep all three sibilants and lenite only by voicing, in decreasing degree from the Gāndhārī Dharmapada to the Niya documents to the inscriptions. Sinhala and Dhivehi start from a Pali-like stage and develop their own lenition.
  • Where compensatory lengthening falls is a major isogloss. It is limited to disyllables or the penult in Hindi, Pahari and Gujarati; to the initial syllable in Marathi, the Bhil lects, Bihari, Bengali, Assamese and Odia, where round 2 also found it blocked before a heavy syllable in Rajasthani–Gujarati; absent in the Northwest, Dardic, Insular and Romani. Adding it to any Northwest lect costs +0.03 to +0.07 NED.
  • Several classic subgroupings fall out of the rule files without being built in. Examples: Kamarupi (Assamese, Kamta, Rajbanshi, Surjapuri, Hajong, Bishnupriya) by ḍ > r; Central vs Eastern Pahari; Shina proper by tr > ʦ̣; the Northwest by no lengthening + post-nasal voicing + rt > ṭṭ; the Bhil lects as Gujarati–Rajasthani rather than Marathi; Halbi and Bhatri as central/eastern rather than Marathi.
  • Romani left the Central continuum early and then spent time in the Northwest. Grafting the Hindi MIA block onto any Romani chain costs +0.054 to +0.087 NED. Romani shares early Central innovations (ts > cʰ, kṣ > kʰ) but not the geminate package. Its north-western traits (post-nasal voicing, t > l, aspirate devoicing) look areal. Domari and Lomavren are separate, more Central exits.
  • OIA hides little of Nuristani. An oracle that knew which branch of each merged PIIr palatal (ś, j, h, kṣ) to use recovers only 1.5–2.3% of the residual error beyond chance. Part of the j split is even recoverable from OIA vowel context. Sound correspondences also flag about 100 Nuristani etyma as likely Indo-Aryan loans (93% precision on a sanity set).
  • Some changes are shared across distant groups and look areal. Examples: stop + r → a lateral (West Pahari ṭ͡ḷ, Kohistani/Kunar/Pashai ɬ/l, Sauji); s > h before a later c > s that escapes it (Bhil, south-western Rajasthani, Assamese); nasal + voiced stop assimilation before nasal vowels form (Pahari, Bihari, eastern Tharu).
  • Most remaining error is not sound change. Gender and extension suffixes (-ā, -ī, -o, -u) are the largest residual in almost every NIA lect. Citation morphology, compounds, learned vocabulary and mixed transcriptions account for most of the rest. Distinct attested forms of the same etymon in Kohistani already differ from each other by 0.42–0.59 NED.
  • The run surfaced many data problems worth fixing in Jambu. Examples: a Rajasthani wordlist filed under Punjabi, Kannauji forms under Hindi, Domaaki classed as Punjabic when its sound changes are Shinaic, Sanskrit headwords and English/German glosses in reflex fields, and a mangled n/a sequence in several Dardic and West Pahari sources. See the curation list.

STAGED:
A staged hypothesis

Putting the order evidence together with what each group found (the counts below compare each lect's own rules for a process, e.g. its own lenition rule against its own degemination rule; they do not claim the rules are the same change, and the rule-level consensus above never pools them), the best-supported history of the family's sound changes runs as follows. Stages are relative, and each branch leaves the sequence at a different point.

I. Early MIA (shared by all Indo-Aryan)

ai au > ē ō; r̩ > a/i/u (ri after consonants in Pali, Dardic and some Pahari); loss of final consonants; ty dy > cc jj, which bled the general C + y assimilation (90 lects for, 1 against); the sibilant merger to s, which fed s + stop > aspirated geminate (85 : 1) and kṣ > kkʰ; then assimilation of stop + stop, r + C and C + sonorant into geminates, and the law of two morae. The Kharoṣṭhī north-west (Gāndhārī, Niya) kept the three sibilants and some clusters; Dardic and Nuristani simplified clusters without making geminates.

II. Prakrit lenition

Aspirates > h, ṭ > ḍ, p > v, loss of single intervocalic stops with ya-śruti, n > ṇ. Pali and Aśokan lack all of it; the Kharoṣṭhī texts only voice; Sinhala has its own, later lenition that keeps d and b. Everywhere it applies, it precedes degemination (stop loss: 120 : 0; aspirate > h: 83 : 0; ṭ > ḍ: 114 : 0), so geminates were protected.

III. Late MIA / Apabhraṁśa

Shortening of final -ā (seen in the eastern, Bihari, Hindi, north-western and Marathi chains, always before apocope and before the -aka > -ā contraction); contraction of aya > ē, which the MIA chains show was a verb-paradigm change rather than a phonological one; hiatus contraction after stop loss (126 : 0).

IV. Early NIA

Degemination, with compensatory lengthening in the Central, Eastern and Southern lects (on the penult or the first syllable, depending on the region) and without it in the Northwest, Dardic and Insular. Before degemination, several singleton-only changes had to happen: l > r (Hindi east, Bihari, Sindhi), l > ḷ (Gujarati–Rajasthani, Marathi, Odia, West Pahari), ṇṇ > nn. Nasal + voiced stop assimilation (mb > mm, ŋg > ŋ) happened before nasal vowels formed in Pahari and Bihari. Anusvāra > nasal vowel. The flap ḍ > ṛ came before degemination in the west and after it in Bihari, Bengali and Hindi-Urdu.

V. Late NIA

Loss of final short vowels, after compensatory lengthening (45 : 2); merger of i/u length after lengthening in the eastern lects; syncope (before or after apocope depending on region); v- > b-, y- > j-, ṇ > n in the Hindi and eastern area; debuccalisation of s, which is several different changes: unconditioned s > h in the Bhil lects and Wagri; s > h between vowels in Punjabi, Lahnda, Sindhi and Dhivehi; initially and between vowels in Mewari, Godwari and Wadiyara Koli; ś > h after a vowel in Assamese and word-initially in Hajong and Bishnupriya. In three groups it is older than a later c > s.
R2_TEXT:
Round 1 only proposed changes conditioned on neighbouring segments, so vowels were under-explored. For round 2 the engine gained syllable-level contexts (C*, first and final syllable, next vowel), built-in Acc/Long/Short classes, and word-level flags (if:verb, if:numeral, if:starred, if:accented). A new probe tool tabulates every OIA vowel's outcome by accent, position, syllable weight and the following vowel. The same 12 groups then audited their round-1 chains and tested the Vedic accent directly, adopting a rule only when it improved held-out training words (leave-one-out) and read as a sound change.

0.451 → 0.443median test NED, all 151 chains
87 / 19lects better / worse on test by ≥ 0.0005
9.9% → 10.8%median exact match on test
5,481 → 5,692rules in all chains

The gains are small and the tuning was done on training data only. Six lects got worse on test by more than 0.005, each traced to a handful of words: Wadiyara Koli (+0.020, one word: *matsiya > maccʰī, predicted mās), Welsh Romani (+0.011, three pairs hit by the Romani a > e rule), Kullui (+0.010, final -i loss hits ákṣi seven times), Dogri (a rule removed once its value fell below zero), Poguli (one verb the verb flag misses) and Kvari (one test item). The rules stay because training data support them.

Scoring changes are reported separately. In four southern Dardic lects the tones marked in the sources were stripped before scoring (%gold-drop tone), since no chain can predict them. This alone accounts for most of their round-2 gain: Maiya 0.612 → 0.552 (the new rules add only −0.010), Gowro −0.031, Bhateri −0.014, Bashkarik −0.002. No other group used it.

What the vowel rules found

  • Lengthening follows NIA syllable structure. Compensatory and pre-anusvāra lengthening happen in the first syllable only when the next syllable is final or light (Rajasthani–Gujarati), only in disyllables or the modern stressed syllable (Hindi belt: áŋgāra > ãgār but píṇḍa > pī̃ḍ), or only in the first syllable (Bengali, as already in Assamese and Odia).
  • Shortening counts syllables, not stress. Long vowels shorten three or more syllables from the end in Hindi (ānāyayati > anānā) and Bihari, two or more in Braj and several West Pahari lects.
  • Final vowels drop only in polysyllables in all 12 southern Dardic lects and Tregami; final -i is lost in parts of West Pahari; final -ī is lost across Nuristani except Waigali.
  • New isoglosses: Bhil-core medial u > a; Kati–Kamviri ā > o and a > u; Romani a > e (Welsh, Balkan, Zargari); Assamese ō > u before a high vowel; Odia V m V > nasal vowel; Prasun first-syllable i-umlaut; Dhivehi u > i before i.
  • Vocalic r̩: a neighbouring labial favours u everywhere, but no accent rule for r̩ survives outside two tiny ones (Sinhala pretonic r̩ > i, Marathi tonic ŕ̩ > i). Apparent accent effects on r̩, and on the -ā/-o citation vowel, turn out to be starred vs Vedic headwords: Turner's reconstructions are never accented and are mostly late -aka formations.

Conventions reconciled after round 2

The 12 agents had coined 122 group-specific tags, many naming the same process. reconcile.py merged 89 of them into 31 shared tags across 137 files, leaving 33 that really are local (tags are comments, and every file was re-scored to confirm identical train NED). 55 notation rules that sat mid-chain were moved to the end with no score change; 26 stay where they are because later rules depend on them (headword normalisation, Awadhi's macron drop before compensatory lengthening, Nuristani placeholder vowels). Citation-vowel rules keyed to Turner's starred headwords are tagged as morphology in every lect, so they no longer count as sound changes in the chronology or the maps.

Marathi, Konkani and Bhil

17 lects · Marathi 0.372, Halbi 0.339, Konkani 0.452

  • The Bhil lects are Gujarati–Rajasthani in type (masculine -o, s > h, nasal clusters kept); the Nimadi chain fits them better than the Marathi one.
  • In Noiri, Dungra Bhil, Wagri and Pauri Bareli, s > h precedes c > s: the new s escaped debuccalisation.
  • Halbi and Bhatri side with Hindi and Odia; nothing specifically Marathi survives.
  • Compensatory lengthening fits the first syllable, not the penult, in Marathi and most Bhil lects.
  • Old Marathi (Tulpule) is mostly learned vocabulary (18% of pairs within 0.2 NED of the Sanskrit), so it gives no chronology.

Bihari and Tharu

17 lects · Bhojpuri 0.298 (30% exact), Maithili 0.337, Bihari 0.391

  • No Magadhan ś anywhere in the data.
  • Nasal + voiced stop: kept in western Tharu; assimilated early in the Bihari core (before nasal vowels); NN in eastern Tharu, Danuwar and Majhi (bandʰa > bān).
  • Compensatory lengthening precedes apocope (+0.012 to +0.025); l > r precedes degemination across Bihari and Tharu.
  • Bote and Majhi show eastern phonology with a Nepali overlay; Dangaura's "e > yā" is one transcriber's on-glide, not a sound change.

Eastern

Odia 0.322, Bengali 0.336, Assamese 0.353, Bishnupriya 0.247 (38% exact)

  • Kamarupi (Assamese, Kamta, Rajbanshi, Surjapuri, Hajong, Bishnupriya) is marked by ḍ > r rather than ṛ. Assamese data fit the Rajbanshi chain better than the Bengali one.
  • Bengali across its stages: the flap and nasal vowels appear between Old and Middle Bengali; loss of final -a comes after Middle Bengali, so the apocope Bengali shares with Assamese is parallel.
  • i/u length merger follows compensatory lengthening in every eastern lect (+0.017 to +0.034); Assamese ś > x/h precedes c > s.
  • Magadhan a > ɔ is invisible in CDIAL, whose eastern forms are orthographic transliterations.

Nuristani

Proto-Nuristani 0.440, Kamviri 0.521, Kati 0.542, Prasun 0.640

  • One ordered history across all seven: palatal and cluster archaisms, then deaspiration, then intervocalic loss, then cluster simplification, then final-vowel loss.
  • Tree: {Kati, Kamviri} vs {Waigali, Tregami} vs Ashkun vs Prasun; a shared initial r- fortition with a different output in each lect.
  • See below for what OIA can and cannot predict.
NOVEL:
• aya > ē is morphological. Restricting it to -ayati/-ayatē verbs beats the general rule in Prakrit, Pali and Gāndhārī, and Aśokan lacks it altogether.
  • Kharoṣṭhī lenition is graded by register: Gāndhārī Dharmapada > Niya documents > inscriptions (none), and all stop at voicing.
  • Insular lenition is not Prakritic. Sinhala keeps d and b, and loses intervocalic d before j > d; Old Sinhala shows no stop loss at all.
  • Khowar vowel harmony. First-syllable a > o when the next syllable has short a (95 : 36), which replaced an accent-based rule; the data also suggest rounding before u/ō and i > e before i. Tested as rules, the rounding before u/ō was adopted (Khowar-only; a closed second syllable blocks it, which fits weight-sensitive stress, but long ō still triggers it), i > e before i was kept but is weak, and an i-umlaut a > e before front vowels in Kalasha and Khowar was rejected: it exists at a 20–25% rate but a categorical rule costs more than it gains.
  • A Cr > lateral isogloss links West Pahari (ṭ͡ḷ), Kohistani/Kunar/Pashai (ɬ, l) and Sauji (tr > ɬ, dr > l), and West Pahari tr > c goes through it.
  • pr > ʦ̣ in Indus Kohistani and Bhateri (pralabʰatē > ʦ̣ālǎṽ), implying a general *Cr > retroflex affricate before the labial was lost.
  • The -aka final vowel survives in Kohistani only where apocope preceded hiatus contraction, an order that splits the Swat lects from Indus Kohistani and Gowro.
  • West Pahari a > ɔ is weight-conditioned, blocked before a following long ā (kaṭāha > kəṛā́) and older than degemination.
  • Hindi l > r is not a West/East split: Braj goes with Awadhi, and Khari Boli with Haryanvi keeps l.
  • Stress-conditioned lengthening before anusvāra in Gujarati (ā̃gaṇ, kā̃ṭɔ vs ãgār, ãdʰārũ), and sk/ṣk > unaspirated kk in several Rajasthani lects, which looks like the Prakrit sukka ~ sukkha doublet surviving.
  • Counter-feeding s > h before c > s recurs in three independent areas (Bhil, south-western Rajasthani/Koli, Assamese).
  • Sindhi degemination is later than its implosives, and gemination in the Northwest is partly a transcription variable: CDIAL writes geminates in 13–17% of Punjabi/Lahnda reflexes, the phonetic wordlists almost never.
  • -triṁśat numerals keep tr in every eastern lect (Bengali ektris, Assamese ektrix, Odia ekatrisa), against Hindi ikattīs: a learned or compound-boundary effect.
  • Western Tharu keeps voiced nasal clusters and has weak lengthening, matching an Awadhi–Bhojpuri affiliation, while eastern Tharu, Danuwar and Majhi share the Bengali–Assamese NN outcome.
  • Two-mora shortening is invisible in NIA in four separate groups, for the same reason each time: compensatory lengthening restores the length it removed.
SPECIAL:
Nuristani: what OIA can predict

Nuristani is not descended from OIA, so these chains are correspondence rules read from the OIA side. They still behave like a single ordered history, and they give a direct answer to how much of Nuristani is inferable from OIA.

The palatal problem is small

OIA merged PIIr contrasts that Nuristani keeps: ś (Nuristani ʦ, or ś in loans), j (ʣ or j), h (ʣ or j) and kṣ (three outcomes). An oracle that picks the right branch per etymon recovers 2.3% of the residual error in Proto-Nuristani, 1.9% in Kati and 1.5% in Kamviri and Waigali, after subtracting what a control oracle over meaningless alternatives gains by chance. About a third of the affected etyma would be better with the other branch, but they are few. The residual is dominated by derivation and compounds in the cited forms, unpredictable vowels (Kati and Kamviri ā ~ o, u ~ ɨ) and mixed transcriptions.

Part of the j split is recoverable from OIA itself: j > ʣ before a/ā, with j kept before front vowels, beats an unconditioned rule in four lects. OIA j before front vowels mostly continues PIIr *ǰ from the second palatalisation.

Loans and inherited words

CDIAL's Nuristani links are stored as neutral groupings. Diagnostic sounds (ś kept rather than ʦ, aspirates, h > ʣ, j > ʣ, cʰ > ʦ) classify about 100 etyma as likely Indo-Aryan loans and 160 as inherited. On a sanity set, 99.6% of strict "inherited" verdicts are core vocabulary and 93% of strict "loan" verdicts (numerals aside) are culture words: oath, guest, country, adze, trap, spear, stable, rice, cat. Loan rates are similar across lects (about 30%); the difference between sources is larger (Turner/Morgenstierne 26–42%, Strand 18–27%), which suggests Turner linked Nuristani words mainly when they looked Indo-Aryan. Whole-chain comparison against Dardic chains barely separates the strata (AUC 0.53–0.57). Caveats: initial ś- before a liquid may be inherited (śarád), Persian loans mimic the archaisms (sahásra > āzor), and wanderwörter are classified by shape only.

Romani and Domari

Verdict: Central origin, early exit, then a north-western period. Replacing a migratory chain's MIA block with the Hindi one costs +0.087 (European Romani), +0.066 (Welsh), +0.071 (Balkan), +0.072 (Lomavren), +0.060 (Zargari) and +0.054 (Domari). Romani shares with Central/NW MIA the innovations ts/ps > cʰ, medial kṣ > kʰ, ava > o, r̩ > i/u and medial syncope, none of which are Dardic. It shares with Dardic only retentions: s + stop and stop + r kept (trin, drak, pʰral), no gemination, no nasal vowels.

The dental lenition is the key clue. Intervocalic t/d became l (Domari r) rather than disappearing, and this had to happen before clusters simplified (+0.003 to +0.008), so geminate tt stayed t (mattá > mato). The ancestors left after -t- had weakened but before the Central loss of intervocalic stops. The north-western traits (post-nasal voicing, found in 0 of 10 Central chains but 10 of 12 Northwest; aspirate devoicing with Pothwari and Dogri parallels; ṣ > ś with s kept, as in West Pahari) are the kind of change easily shared through contact.

Whole-chain scores alone do not settle this: raw scores favour the Kalasha chain, but after normalising length, nasal vowels and geminates, the Hindi, Punjabi, Lahnda and Shina chains all fit European Romani within about 0.01. Domari is the most Central in its obstruents (s-merger, velar loss) and lacks the Romani aspirate devoicing (adding it costs +0.02); its closest outside chain is Domaaki. Lomavren adds Central/NW changes Romani lacks (st > tʰ, voiced aspirate > h), consistent with a later exit.

Transcription and tooling

  • Several field sources need source-level notation metadata (written length, dentals written with the retroflex underdot, digraph aspirates); the agents' %source blocks record them.
  • The CDIAL profile splits accented diphthongs (saínya, saúvarṇa; 31 sequences among 18,527 etyma), and U+01DD ǝ is not folded like ə.
  • Nuristani loan/inherited candidates are in results/nuristani-strata.csv for review.
METHOD:
Data. For every lect with at least 100 etyma linked to a CDIAL Indo-Aryan headword by an inherited reflex edge (borrowings excluded), the reflex pairs were extracted from cldf/forms.csv and cldf/edges.csv: 153 lects, of which the unspecified "MIA" lect was dropped as unusable (fragments and OIA forms) and Sanskrit and Proto-Indo-Iranian were not targets. Nuristani (7 lects) was included as a sister branch. Pairs are split 80/20 by a stable hash of the etymon, so an etymon is in the same split for every lect.

Rules. Each lect has an ordered rule file in a small sound-change language: segments from Jambu's grapheme profile, classes, sets, back-references with feature modifiers ($1-asp, $1+long), environments with optional elements and exceptions, and per-source notation blocks. Every rule carries one or more tags from a shared catalogue (@int-stop-loss, @degem-lengthen …), which is what makes rules comparable across lects.

Metric. Normalised edit distance (NED) over segments between the predicted and the attested form, averaged over reflex pairs, plus exact-match rate. Stress marks, homonym digits and a few lax-vowel letters are normalised on the attested side only.

Process. Twelve agents, one per group of lects, wrote and hill-climbed the chains on the training split only, using per-rule leave-one-out value, residual confusions and a rule-suggestion tool, and kept only rules that read as plausible sound changes. Two baselines: no rules (the etymon itself) and a greedy induction that adds, one at a time, the single-segment change that most reduces training NED. Every chain was then ablated (rules removed greedily, least useful first) to get a rules-vs-score curve.

Chronology. For each pair of rules i before j in a chain, two moves reverse them: j to just before i, and i to just after j. If both raise training NED, the lect requires i before j; if both lower it, the reverse fits better. Results are pooled by tag across lects.

These chains are models of the data, not reconstructions. A rule that improves NED can be a real sound change, a transcription convention, or a regularity of citation form. Tags mark @notation and @morph rules explicitly, and those are excluded from the chronology and grouping analyses.

Limits

  • Morphology is the ceiling. Gender and extension suffixes, infinitive and other citation forms, and compounds dominate the residual. The most-requested engine feature (7 of 12 groups) is conditioning rules on part of speech or word class; next are source blocks that can run inside the chain (6) and morpheme boundaries (5).
  • Non-local contexts are hard to find. The rule-suggestion tool only proposes changes conditioned on adjacent segments, so vowel harmony, umlaut and stress effects were found only when someone looked for them (Khowar, Kalasha, West Pahari, Gujarati). A correspondence-table view conditioned on the next syllable would help every lect.
  • Small test sets. About 60 lects have fewer than 100 test pairs; their test NED moves by ±0.01–0.05 with single words. Train numbers are steadier.
  • Orders are only as good as the chains. An order is evidence only where both single-rule moves hurt, and rules phrased differently can change which orders are testable (for example, lengthening conditioned on a following vowel versus a word-final geminate).
  • Grouping. The tag clustering uses presence and absence, so shared absences pull lects together. Cross-scoring chains on other lects' data, which several groups did locally, is a better tree-building signal but needs notation normalisation.
